New Zealand Braces for Economic Impact as Influenza Outbreak Prompts Nationwide Closures

WELLINGTON, June 14—New Zealand’s government has imposed sweeping public health measures, including the closure of most non-essential businesses and schools, as authorities grapple with the country’s largest influenza epidemic in more than two decades. The outbreak, which has led to thousands of hospitalizations since late May, is causing significant disruption to economic activity nationwide.

Prime Minister Jessica Mahoney announced on Friday that the current restrictions, which include stay-at-home orders for most residents, would remain in place “until public health officials are confident the risk of community transmission has abated.” The measures, which began on June 10, have shuttered retail outlets, construction sites, and many offices, while essential services such as supermarkets and pharmacies remain open under strict hygiene protocols.

Among the companies feeling the effects is Fletcher Building Ltd, one of the country’s largest construction and building materials groups. “The government’s decision to halt most construction activity in urban areas is in line with our top priority—the health and safety of our workers and the public. However, the impact on our operations and the broader sector is significant,” said Fletcher Building spokesperson Susan Lee in a statement.

According to the New Zealand Council of Trade Unions, more than 250,000 workers across multiple industries are directly affected by the closures. “The government must ensure that wage support and sick leave cover everyone who’s been forced to stay home, especially casual and contract workers,” said Council President Timran Patel.

The Ministry of Health on Friday reported that over 12,000 people have been treated for severe influenza symptoms so far, with 1,800 currently hospitalized. Public health experts have urged compliance with the restrictions to slow the virus’s spread. “This is not a typical flu season. The strain we’re seeing is highly transmissible, and the pressure on hospitals is severe,” said Dr. Anika Rawiri, epidemiologist at Wellington Regional Hospital.

Economic analysts estimate that the restrictions could reduce New Zealand’s GDP growth by as much as 1.5% if they remain in place through July. “The construction sector alone accounts for around 6% of national output, and the ripple effects of these closures will be felt in supply chains and local communities,” said Jayson Park, senior economist at Tasman Analytics.

Finance Minister Robyn Ng said the government is preparing a second round of relief measures, including grants for small businesses and expanded support for workers. “Our immediate focus is public health, but we recognize the economic hardship these closures are causing. We’re committed to helping businesses and families weather this storm,” she said.

Officials will review the restrictions in one week, citing the need for further data on infection rates and hospital capacity.
